subject: physics_2
question_text: State Gauss's law in electrostatics and its importance.

mark_split.label: The equation with q and ε₀ named

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: ∮E·dS = q/ε₀ where q is the NET charge enclosed by the closed surface — matches NCERT and the book (printed p.21). The book lists three points under Importance and all three are kept; the condition of symmetry is added to the first, because Gauss's law yields the field quickly only when the distribution is symmetric enough that E is constant over the chosen surface — without that the integral cannot be taken out. The book prints 'permitivity' (p.20) and 'permittivity of free spaced' (p.19); both are written correctly here. This chapter also carries a 2-mark VSAQ, ts_ipe_p2_ecf_gauss_law_statement, that asks the statement alone; the two cards are the book's own separate questions, not a duplication.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Statement of Gauss's law
lines: Gauss's law: the total electric flux through
any closed surface is 1/ε₀ times the net
charge enclosed by that surface.
Here ε₀ is the permittivity of free space.
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words closed surface, net charge and enclosed all have to appear.
steps.why: Each word in the statement is doing work: the surface must be closed, the charge must be the net charge, and it must be inside. Charges outside the surface add nothing to the total flux.
common_mistakes: Saying every charge nearby. Only the charge enclosed by the surface counts.
Writing flux = qε₀. It is q divided by ε₀.

recall.must_convey: That the total flux through any closed surface equals 1/ε₀ times the net charge enclosed.
accept: total electric flux through a closed surface
one by epsilon nought times the charge enclosed
reject: applicable for any shape and size

steps.memory_tip: Three words carry the statement: closed, net, enclosed.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: A closed surface S of any shape with the charge q inside, a small area element dS on it, and the field E through that element.
steps.why: The integral in the law is a sum over small pieces of the surface, so the figure has to show one such piece dS and the field E crossing it — that is what E·dS means.
common_mistakes: Drawing an open sheet. The surface in Gauss's law must be closed.
Putting the charge outside the surface. Then the enclosed charge is zero.

recall.must_convey: That the figure shows a closed surface S with charge q inside, an area element dS and the field E through it.
accept: draw a closed surface with the charge inside
mark a small area element dS
show the field arrow through the element
reject: flux equals q by epsilon nought

steps.memory_tip: One closed loop, one charge inside, one small patch with an arrow through it.

steps.label: The equation
lines: Mathematically,
Here q is the total charge enclosed by the
closed surface S, and dS is a small area
element of that surface. The circle on the
integral sign shows the surface is closed.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. The equation alone is not enough — name q, S and dS under it.
steps.why: The equation is the statement written in symbols, so every symbol in it must be tied back to the words: the circle on the integral is the word closed, and q is the word enclosed.
common_mistakes: Leaving the circle off the integral sign. It is what makes the surface closed.
Writing E dS instead of E · dS. It is a dot product, so only the part of E across the surface counts.

recall.must_convey: That the law in symbols is ∮E·dS = q/ε₀, with q the enclosed charge and dS an area element of the closed surface S.
accept: closed integral of E dot dS
q is the charge enclosed by the surface
reject: one by epsilon nought times the charge enclosed

steps.memory_tip: Circle on the integral = closed surface; the letter after the equals sign is always the enclosed charge.

steps.label: Importance: finding the field
steps.mark_note: Gives E for symmetric charge distributions
lines: Importance:
1. It gives the electric field intensity of
charged bodies whose charge distribution is
symmetric — a long straight wire, a large
charged sheet, a charged spherical shell —
far more quickly than Coulomb's law does.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Name the use and give at least one body it is used on.
steps.why: Coulomb's law needs the field of every element added up by integration. Gauss's law replaces that with one surface integral, and when the distribution is symmetric E is the same size all over the chosen surface, so it comes out of the integral in one line.
common_mistakes: Saying it works for every charge distribution. The law is always true, but it gives E easily only when there is enough symmetry.
Listing no example. One named body earns the mark.

recall.must_convey: That Gauss's law is used to find the field of symmetric charge distributions, such as a wire, a sheet or a shell.
accept: to find the electric intensity of charged bodies
used for a wire a sheet or a sphere
reject: true for any shape and size of surface

steps.memory_tip: Wire, sheet, shell — the three bodies Gauss's law is always used on.

steps.label: Importance: how general it is
steps.mark_note: Any closed surface; charges at rest or moving
lines: 2. It holds for a closed surface of any
shape and any size, so you can pick a
surface that suits the symmetry of the
problem.
3. It applies to charges at rest and to
moving charges as well.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Two separate points: any surface, and moving charges too.
steps.why: The freedom to pick the surface is what makes the law useful, and it is a freedom only because the law puts no condition on the shape or the size. Its validity for moving charges is what carries it into the rest of electromagnetism.
common_mistakes: Saying the surface must be a sphere. Any closed shape works.
Saying it holds only for charges at rest. It holds for moving charges too.

recall.must_convey: That the law holds for a closed surface of any shape and size, and for moving charges as well as charges at rest.
accept: any shape and any size of closed surface
we can choose a convenient surface
reject: used to find the field of a wire or a sheet

steps.memory_tip: Two freedoms: any surface, and charges need not be at rest.

insider_note: The question asks for two things — the law and its importance — so a script that stops after the integral can score only half.
